public_rationale: Marcus said that in January 2025 there was still no principled, trustworthy answer to AI hallucination. A Nature news feature from 21 January 2025 was headlined 'AI hallucinations can't be stopped — but these techniques can limit their damage'. It said language models were still struggling to tell the truth. OpenAI's o3-mini system card, for a model launched in late January 2025, reported a 14.8% hallucination rate on PersonQA. OpenAI said more work was needed to understand hallucinations. The best principled method I found, semantic entropy (Nature, 2024), detects only a subset of hallucinations and does not prevent them. The evidence shows that ways to reduce or partly detect hallucinations existed, but no accepted, reliable solution did. Only the factual part of the sentence is scored, not his view that reliable agents need this problem solved.
limitations: 'Principled trustworthy answer' is not defined. Someone could argue that methods like semantic entropy or grounding in retrieved documents are partial principled answers.
The body of the Nature feature was paywalled; the assessment relies on its headline, standfirst and a summary.
The claim that reliable agents need hallucination solved is a premise and was not assessed.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: As of January 2025 there is no principled, trustworthy solution to the hallucination problem.

statement.excerpt: That is in part because you can’t build reliable agents unless you can solve the hallucination problem, and there is still no principled trustworthy answer to that problem.
statement.document_title: AI Agents: Hype versus Reality, redux

from_speaker: there is still no principled trustworthy answer
you can't build reliable agents unless you can solve the hallucination problem
our_interpretation: Only the factual part is scored: that as of January 2025 no method existed that reliably and verifiably eliminated or solved hallucinations in generative AI / LLMs. The claim that reliable agents require solving hallucination is a premise about what agents need and is not scored.

Plain reading of 'principled trustworthy answer': a method, grounded in theory, that reliably prevents or removes hallucinations across general use, so that outputs can be trusted. Methods that only reduce hallucination rates, or detect some of them, do not count as such an answer.
Target period: January 2025, the month of the post. The post describes an ongoing state ('still no') without naming a period.
criteria.support_condition: Expert or primary sources from around January 2025 say hallucinations had not been eliminated or reliably solved, or frontier models of that time still showed large measured hallucination rates.
criteria.contradiction_condition: A method existed by January 2025 that was widely accepted, or independently shown, to reliably eliminate hallucinations in general-purpose LLMs.

evidence.excerpt: Developers have tricks to stop artificial intelligence from making things up, but large language models are still struggling to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.
evidence.locator: standfirst, under headline 'AI hallucinations can't be stopped — but these techniques can limit their damage'
evidence.explanation: A major science journal's survey of the field in January 2025 says hallucinations can't be stopped and that existing techniques only limit the damage. That matches 'no principled trustworthy answer'.

evidence.excerpt:
More work is needed to understand hallucinations holistically, particularly in domains not covered
by our evaluations (e.g., chemistry).
evidence.locator: section 4.1.3 Hallucination Evaluations, Table 3 (PersonQA hallucination rate: 52.4% GPT-4o-mini, 27.4% o1-mini, 14.8% o3-mini)
evidence.explanation: OpenAI's newest model at the end of January 2025 still hallucinated on 14.8% of PersonQA questions, and OpenAI said more work was needed to understand hallucinations. No general solution was in hand.

evidence.excerpt: Vempala and others are working on ways to make hallucinations less frequent and less problematic.
evidence.publisher: Georgia Institute of Technology, College of Computing
evidence.explanation: Summary of the Nature feature. It shows that researchers' goal in January 2025 was to reduce hallucinations, not that they had solved them.

evidence.excerpt: Here we develop new methods grounded in statistics, proposing entropy-based uncertainty estimators for LLMs to detect a subset of hallucinations—confabulations—which are arbitrary and incorrect generations.
evidence.explanation: The strongest counterpoint I found: a principled, theory-grounded method from 2024. But it only detects a subset of hallucinations and does not prevent them, so it is not a full trustworthy answer.
